messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 69-year-old male with a known duodenal diverticulum and remote history of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery, was admitted to the hospital with bilateral upper quadrant abdominal pain for several weeks, nausea, abdominal distension, and food intolerance. A CT scan revealed a distended gastric remnant and a possible bowel obstruction.

The patient was taken to the operating room for an exploratory laparotomy where a 4.5 cm enterolith was found and removed from the distal jejunum. A cholecystectomy was also performed during which gallstones were discovered. The patient had an uneventful recovery and was discharged on postoperative day 8.

Follow-up:
At the patient's postoperative visit, two weeks after surgery, he was reported to be in good health. Unfortunately, the patient was lost to follow-up after one month.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Summary:
This 69-year-old male presented with bilateral upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, abdominal distension, and food intolerance. He was found to have a distended gastric remnant and a bowel obstruction caused by a 4.5 cm enterolith containing bile salts. Treatment included an exploratory laparotomy and enterolith removal, as well as a cholecystectomy. The patient had an uneventful recovery and was discharged on postoperative day 8. It is unfortunate that the patient was lost to follow-up after one month.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The admission was chiefly for small bowel obstruction caused by a 4.5 cm enterolith impacted in the distal jejunum, which was removed at laparotomy. This is an intestinal obstruction from impaction, which belongs to chapter K (digestive system). It falls under category K56 (paralytic ileus and intestinal obstruction without hernia); the gallstones and cholecystectomy are secondary.

CODE: K56
